children.translated_text: <s>Ātmakhyāti</s> (self-manifestation), <s>asatkhyāti</s> (manifestation of the non-existent),
<s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension), and <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (otherwise-apprehension) —
among the examiners, regarding illusion,
because of dispute, it is discriminated.
The non-existent does not shine — not a sky-
An object appears; therefore cognition
has its form — so say some.
As long as it is impossible,
let that much be abandoned;
the abandonment of the form of the experienced
does not qualify as illusion.
When a sublator is conceived
through partial sublation,
total sublation is not appropriate —
thus hold those who know logic.
Another [object] appearing externally
does not deserve to be held internally;
non-existence is preferable for it,
for that is consistent with its being illusory.
Illusion is not [established] by internal existence,
but is to be accepted through non-existence;
therefore, not positing [it] internally,
[the proponent] indeed posited non-existence.
The appearance of internal [content] as external
is not possible because of [its] being illusory;
when that is posited through non-existence alone,
[the cognition] indeed does not possess valid means of knowledge.
Of what appears as such,
non-existence must necessarily be posited;
and even if there is internal existence,
illusion in external existence is not possible.
From non-apprehension without distinction,
there would be illusion even in deep sleep;
indeed, non-apprehension exists there too,
and non-apprehension is not distinguished [in that case].
There is no basis for reproach —
the manifestation of the non-existent here;
therefore, since this is the cause of illusion,
the same would apply in correct cognition.
Otherwise-apprehension is not appropriate
in illusion without a substrate;
for in dreams, illusion without a substrate
is beyond doubt.
If there too, what is not present
is grasped as if present,
the non-existence of the non-present
is not different from a sky-flower.
Of things utterly not experienced,
which are mutually dissimilar,
and of what is not present as seen —
there is no manifestation as if present.
What manifestation is there for something equal to a sky-flower,
since it appears without any form?
Yet even that serves practical purposes,
since it appears as having form.
But even in such a supposition,
there is no avoidance of the manifestation of the non-existent;
the connection with another mode —
indeed the non-existent simply appears.
Therefore this appearance
of the non-existent as having form
must necessarily be posited,
and because of the simplicity of this supposition.
The impression from prior knowledge of that reality,
its awakening with a cause,
the error of 'I remember' —
that is the cause for one whose senses are engaged.
In illusion, the defectiveness of the mind
together with the senses is internally transformed,
in intense desire, death,
fainting, grief, illness, and so forth.
Even in destroying [circumstances], the extensive
continuation of the impression [is observed];
in opposing positions, what must be supposed
is mostly [already] seen.
Since death interrupts, cutting off
all impressions, resulting in non-remembrance,
what was experienced in a previous birth
is not remembered — thus it is established.
Cooperating with a weak impression,
in its interruption, with or without it,
the mind damaged by defects is to be made to function
devoid of resolution and the like.
Unaltered by defects, healthy,
equipped with resolution and the like —
it does not function like [a defective mind] in waking;
oh, the extreme [position] of those who know logic!
The damage by defects exists
in the form of the loss of capacity to function,
and there is an excess of effect too —
oh, such discrimination of logic!
In superimposition, it would be secondary,
like [the cognition of] a cow applied to a <s>Vāhīka</s> [non-cow];
there would be no conformity to cognition
if there is no discriminating understanding.
Non-apprehension too
does not conform to cognition, since the understanding
through co-referentiality
'this is silver' is established.
Therefore, 'this is indeed illusion' —
this determination is appropriate;
the cause of it
following cognition is not tenable.
Therefore, those who know <s>Brahman</s> recognize
the indescribability —
the <s>avidyā</s>-nature (ignorance-nature) of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance);
otherwise, [the theory] is undermined.
If existent, it is not false; if void,
manifestation is difficult to explain;
indescribable as either existent or non-existent —
that is how they speak of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
The search for an entity within it,
whether external or internal,
is not appropriate anywhere,
because of the destruction of that in the knowable object.
This proliferation of name and form
is described as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) itself;
but in the otherwise-apprehension of another,
there is no denial of proliferation.
In non-apprehension, it would be mere void —
on what basis would proliferation [exist]?
The non-proliferated appearing as having
the form of proliferation — this is tenable.
In the non-apprehension of the unclear,
granted — let it not appear clearly by itself;
but in the superimposition of what does not exist,
diversity is pointlessly created.
In consciousness of diverse forms,
since it has the nature of proliferation itself,
there would be no liberation;
or else impermanence would follow.
In illusion of multiple forms,
such as <s>gandharvanagara</s> (mirage cities) and the like,
the forms of a single
unreal cognition clearly shine.
The form of consciousness is not an element,
nor are superimposition and unclear apprehension [adequate];
the nature of transformation in illusions —
therefore this is the view of those who know <s>Brahman</s>.
Because the manifestation of the non-existent is impossible,
because of contradiction with cognition, another [thinker],
thinking himself clever, declared
illusion to be correct apprehension.
'Nothing appears' — and [yet something does];
this appears contradictory;
in appearing as having form,
[the object is] not non-existent, because of contradiction with cognition.
The otherwise-apprehension of another
is therefore not tenable either;
that one thing appears and another
is grasped — this is extremely difficult to maintain.
An object-support is not [established]
merely by causality, since in the sense organ too that [applies];
an object-support is not established
merely by causality alone.
And if cognition appears differently
from the form of the object-support,
then it would indeed be without an object-support,
because of the departure from its defining characteristic.
And thus, for [cognition] having that nature,
there is no determination of the reality of the object;
even though dependent, if it lacks
a graspable [object], it is non-cognizing.
Because of the suspicion of being memory, there is no
certainty regarding the present [object] here;
since non-apprehension of distinction
when the cause is present is not possible.
When the cause is impaired, indeed that [non-apprehension occurs];
in its absence, there is clear apprehension;
and from the effort of non-perception,
and in its absence, there is certainty.
Similarity, having been seen, reflection, and so forth
are awakeners of the seed of memory;
and because of the error of 'I remember,'
mostly [this is] perceptual illusion.
If absolutely existent, what illusion is there?
If non-existent, what is manifested?
Because it accords with both, <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (otherwise-apprehension)
is approved by the elders.
Where nothing is manifest,
there certainly is no illusion;
as in deep sleep — just as the earth's shadow
and darkness are perceived [without illusion].
The incorrect manifestation of two [things]
or of one is considered illusion;
what then is this incorrectness?
An ineptitude residing in cognition.
Or else, the non-apprehension of all modes
and the apprehension of some —
of an object in a mode not its own —
but such manifestation is not accepted.
In that case, regarding what is distant or subtle,
there occurs indistinct perception,
or manifestation of the mere universal —
and no illusion is experienced.
And no cognition whatsoever reveals
the object in its entirety;
the falsity of all cognition
would follow, [were it] otherwise.
Therefore, dream cognition is not false
because of [the object's] non-presence in the cognition;
but because of the awareness of being present,
and likewise from the superimposition of identity.
The silver-cognition here is not false
because of the non-ascertainment of distinction;
in the illusion of recognition,
it is not understood as being memory.
And because of the distinctness of one [element],
the distinctness of the other [follows];
and because of non-discrimination from perception,
perceptual illusion is established.
And there may be illusion in the domain of memory
from non-discrimination from what is remembered;
There would be no determinate activity
if otherwise-apprehension is not accepted.
If the difference between the seen and unseen
is not a manifestation of the desired nature —
but surely for us, cognition with reversed object
[is rejected] because of contradiction with experience.
And because of unreliability, the silver-
cognition is memory of silver;
this is not so, for then one would not act
towards the piece of oyster shell.
If that activity is towards [real] silver,
[that is] not [possible] because of its non-proximity;
if because of non-awareness of non-proximity —
then whence the restriction of activity?
That one acts right there [where one is]
is caused by the proximity of that [thing];
elsewhere, because of apprehension of difference,
and likewise because of non-apprehension of distinction.
If the difference in activity due to similarity
is non-apprehension of distinction,
one would act towards unseen [silver]
in clods of earth and the like, due to non-discrimination.
If there is no such cognition there,
then there is none in the oyster shell either;
but if there is a cognition with reversed object,
how can [otherwise-apprehension] be denied?
Non-activity because of not having been seen
is equal in the case of the oyster shell;
that [silver] which was seen, in whatever form —
that is not the cause of activity.
If due to non-discrimination of the seen and the remembered,
let this be examined here:
from the awareness of reality, from the awareness of being apparent,
from the cognition of silver.
Activity towards the seen [object], in the former [case],
[constitutes] the reversed-object nature of the cognition;
the difference between the seen and unseen
is not useful in the latter [case].
For in seeing sky-connection [i.e., transparency],
[the argument] is useful for superimposition;
visual error would not [apply]
to the unseen or unconnected.
If the difference between memory
and the result of valid cognition is accepted,
their respective objects are distinguished —
on what basis then is non-discrimination?
If memory does not distinguish
its own object from another,
then in the perception of a universal, and in the memory
of another, there would always be illusion.
If [you say] due to the discrimination of 'I remember' —
if that is not admitted,
when the results are not different, whence
the understanding of a difference in cognitions inferred from results?
And the cognition 'I remember'
is cited as different from memory;
but it is not different from the result of valid cognition —
that [discrimination] is not established without the result.
If one's own object is not discriminated
by memory due to a mental defect,
then in cases of eye disease and the like, how [would there be]
the illusion of hairs etc. when the mind is healthy?
The mind is not defective there either,
because of discriminating other objects;
for 'having been seen' [is established] from cognition alone,
and because of the cumbersomeness of the supposition.
Perceiving discrimination,
'I see due to a sense defect
paintings and such forms, lamps and the like' —
thus the common people speak.
From the differences in defects of the sense organs,
there are specific observations of illusion;
it would not occur when the defect's operation
is in non-apprehension — thus is the certainty.
And not every illusion
is necessarily caused by similarity;
illusion of yellow in white is observed,
and illusion of bitter in sweet.
And because of obtaining that without [the sense's] engagement —
hence no perception of bile [by the sense];
and the cognition of what is extremely close
is difficult, like collyrium and the like.
And the illusions of double moon and the like
are not born from non-discrimination of cognition-differences
arising from the functioning of the sense organ;
for they are neither in perception nor in memory.
And even when the object-support is otherwise,
cognition is not without an object-support;
for even with another form,
visual cognition does not support the eye [differently].
The meaning of object-support is the fitness
for practical activity appropriate to it;
for even of another [object], 'that is not another,
it is that very one' — thus it has been shown.
And thus the activity towards the oyster shell
of one desiring silver;
and it appears in some manner —
it does not absolutely fail to appear.
Therefore [objection] is not from [mere] appearance; but
because of non-deviation from its form,
validity must be independent indeed —
otherwise it would be a cause of embarrassment.
How is that embarrassing for us,
proponents of intrinsic validity?
Has anyone else through non-deviation
accepted the validity of cognition?
Validity is from awareness itself —
knowing this position of the <s>Mīmāṃsakas</s>,
an unlearned person would reject it
through [the argument from] non-deviation.
If non-deviation with the object [is required],
what is not cognized cannot be validated;
and from the non-deviation of cognition
[to say] 'that is its awareness' — this is untenable.
The non-difference of that cognition
is to be relied upon, similarly or otherwise;
with an unestablished non-difference,
it is being grasped ..........
Moreover, non-difference too
is known through the form of cognition;
and in reversed apprehension,
because of the consequence of contradiction with that.
That being so, let that alone
be the revealer of the object;
the object [is not established] through non-difference,
but through cognition attained by its capacity.
If the rejection of invalidity
is through the non-apprehension of deviation —
when [cognition] is vitiated by deviation,
there would be no validity in cognition.
This [objection] is not valid — validity is not vitiated
by non-deviation for one [whose theory is otherwise];
just as that [inferential mark] is vitiated by deviation
as a logical sign, but not so the sense organ.
That which assumes usefulness
dependent on the knowledge of relation —
that, when vitiated by deviation,
would be a cause of doubt.
What is informative by its mere existence
is not vitiated by deviation;
and the awareness of an object from cognition
is by its mere existence, like the sense organ and the like.
What is obtained through the non-deviation
of the logical sign — that belongs to its form;
one should not lead to causality
[arguments] whose force of conviction is already established.
In validity and in its absence,
non-difference and reversal [are seen];
for thus, non-difference too
has been described as arising from awareness alone.
Difference [arises] from the awareness of sublation —
thus is the accordance with that scripture;
when the capacity of cognition is unestablished,
how can that unestablished [argument] be a refuter?
Even when established, how can established capacity
lead to incapacity?
But if there is deviation,
as agreed by sublating cognition,
the validity of the very form of cognition
would be destroyed by that alone;
'the object is as it appears from the form of cognition' —
this is what is determined.
From the very cognition of deviation,
it is understood that it is not so;
true, sublating cognition
destroys [validity] wherever it operates.
But destruction elsewhere would not be
either directly or even implicitly;
it would be inference, and that too
has its domain removed by that [sublation].
'The cognition does not arise for one who is awake' —
thus is shown in the <s>Bhāṣya</s> (commentary);
from the mere knowledge of deviation,
there is no damage to validity for us.
In what deviates, there is no confidence;
Even in three ways, validity
is not destroyed by deviation;
it has been stated that non-difference
is not the reason for being a valid means of knowledge.
That by whose absence as a cause
there would be reversal in deviation —
even for smoke and the like, that
is not described as [arising] from non-deviation.
In its arising from awareness alone,
its role as a factor is accepted;
for thus, the causality
of non-deviating [cognitions] is from some [source].
When awareness does not arise, someone
does not accept validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>);
awareness determined toward a single object,
even though producing [it], though deviating —
the eye is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>),
occurring in [the cognition of] blue, of the existent, or of white;
nor indeed does deviation
directly destroy validity.
Observed somewhere in erroneous cognition,
the sublating cognition is destructive;
of [properties such as] being a knowable, uprightness, and so forth,
awareness alone is the determiner.
'It does not exist' — [that view] lacks validity (<s>pramāṇatva</s>),
and because of absence of cause, it does not exist;
and because of its existence, validity
belongs to the sense organs, even though they deviate.
And when [the object] is determined, it is not fitting
that doubt should arise from duality;
for even when a post is determined,
they differ only in [its] uprightness.
[...lacuna...]
[...lacuna...]
And not merely from determination
does non-determination of reality [follow].
Since it is thus from that [perspective], therefore not thus —
this would be an excellent statement;
and consciousness, by its very arising,
is the determiner of its being-so.
If not so, then from no other [source] either
is the arising of its validity possible;
validity and invalidity
are not [established through] mutual exclusion and reversal.
Since it is not a factor, thus futile indeed
is the examination of those two here;
therefore, through the deviation of apparent determination,
examination [is conducted].
[Having introduced...] [...lacuna...]
[...lacuna...]
In the absence of cause, absence of effect —
there would be a rule; when that is gone.
In the absence of defects in the cause,
there is the ascertainment of veridical cognition (<s>tathā-khyāti</s>);
the effect is not invariable in the cause
when it depends on transformation and the like.
Therefore, even when the cause is undefective,
there is no certainty of clear apprehension;
direct experience (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is to be established,
not from a deviating cause.
The absence of a contrary result
is established from the absence of cause;
through the cessation of the appropriate effect,
from the establishment of the contrary.
Of defects, the extreme defect —
its existence becomes manifest;
an excess of effect is seen in the belly
and in fire through ashes.
When the mind is disturbed by desire and so forth,
there is seeing in what is [actually] memory;
through co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>),
from the cognition of non-primary silver.
And that awareness is one and undivided —
which position does it refute?
And that it appears as empty —
the two are like contradictions.
In appearing as having form,
emptiness would be called empty indeed;
for the separation from all forms
is spoken of as 'empty'.
When form is accepted by others,
the cognition of emptiness there is empty indeed;
if one thinks that non-existence
appears in the form of existence —
<s>anyathā-khyāti</s> (erroneous cognition as otherwise) alone is accepted;
if that too is considered empty,
these two are not contradictory:
emptiness and having the form of non-existence.
Therefore, its emptiness here
consists merely in its not being of that place and time;
but if a thing exists as it is,
when it appears as such, there is no error.
When it does not appear as it is,
one is not freed from the cognition of emptiness;
some say: from the qualified [things],
the qualifications do not shine forth.
They appear as separate thus,
and the position is that they exist;
others consider emptiness as merely that —
[they say] error is not [cognition of something] as otherwise.
Cognition that is object-based is not [cognition] as otherwise;
without an objective support, it does not exist;
but the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> [<s>Kumārila</s>] himself
has described the resolution here.
Non-existence is another entity; another [entity]
does not exist, because it cannot be characterized;
truly, when [a thing] does not appear as it is,
that appearance is considered error.
Not in the manner in which it exists —
yet it is not cognized as utterly void;
how then could there be non-existence for this?

children.text: sa hi bhāti tathā ca saḥ
children.translated_text: For it appears thus, and it is thus.
For non-existence is another entity
from some perspective;
and in the position of <s>anyathā-khyāti</s> (error as otherwise),
the other qualification is not non-existent.
And [the cognition] is of another, not of that —
the cognition is fitting, and it is false;
[but] the conjunction with another qualification —
does it not appear as simply non-existent?
What is experienced is not the otherness
of another... [...lacuna...]
The conjunction of two distinct [entities] here
does not appear at all.
Cognition of another (<s>anya-khyāti</s>) is through the nature of another;
and in the absence of this, that is false;
the cognition that apprehends absence
depends on another entity.
Separately from that other,
what is indescribable does not exist;
therefore, except as another entity,
because absence there cannot be characterized.
By cognition, emptiness of entity [is not established];
and it is false — thus say the wise;
not even in the case of a hare's horn
is what appears indescribable.
For the form associated with a hare
is understood there as a horn;
and that is not a non-entity, by which
it is seen as having the property of hooves.
That is the absence of what is unconjoined —
thus the cognition is false;
a herd of elephants on the tip of a finger —
such is this intuition likewise.
In dream too, the apprehension of what is not present
is like [the apprehension of] what is present;
nor is there a difference from a sky-flower;
at its own time, that has reality.
For the knowable exists only at that time;
but now there is only cognition;
present-ness too here —
what is seen is perceived elsewhere.
The perception of another too is seen as otherwise,
[even] of mutually contradictory [things];
utter non-experience
exists, since that is produced [thus].
Consciousness is not empty of a knowable object,
because of the undesirable consequence of self-destruction;
from connection with the indescribable self,
and from the non-independence of the mind.
Things possessing valid means of knowledge, though unseen,
are posited, even very many;
of the causes that sever impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>),
the reality is not absolutely established.
And what was experienced in another life
is not remembered — this is established;
the connection of that <s>karma</s> and its result,
one asserts based on dependent [origination].
For thus, in beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s>,
even remembering the varieties of <s>karma</s>,
because of having performed infinite <s>karmas</s>,
who could know which result belongs to which?
The disturbance of one's own mind in dream
is the awakener of the seed of memory;
and because of its absence in the waking state,
dream vision does not arise.
Even when disturbed by desire and so forth, likewise,
an excess of effect has been illustrated;
one grasps what is indeed ungraspable —
for this [mind] itself fabricates.
Of the mind impaired by defects,
that is the effect... [...lacuna...]
In that superimposition (<s>adhyāropa</s>), it is not figurative,
because of the determination 'it is so'.
In the presence [of the substrate], it cognizes as non-empty
[that which is] existent, struck by another entity;
but for those who shine forth, non-existence
is not empty, [for] that is without self.
[...lacuna...]
And thus, <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), which is inexpressible,
is not to be dismissed;
because ignorance (<s>avidyātva</s>) of another
would make it manifest another form.
[...lacuna...]
[...lacuna...]
[...lacuna...]
The falsity of sublated cognition
is not established otherwise;
therefore, as long as it is to be sublated,
that long it is fitting [to call it] false.
And externality in the object of erroneous cognition
is not negated by sublating [cognitions];
internality is not ascertained,
nor is there cognition through inexpressibility.
But what [is established] is its not being of that place and time —
[this] is ascertained of the external object;
therefore, externality as an object
is not false from cognition, nor from sublation.
Sublation, which is in the nature of negation of what is connected,
is not fitting in the <s>akhyāti</s> (non-cognition) [theory];
sublation itself clearly establishes
<s>anyathā-khyāti</s> (erroneous cognition as otherwise) for us.
For <s>akhyāti</s> is not merely a [reductio] consequence
— in our position it is fitting [as a theory];
nor is this a negation of apprehension,
because of the undesirable consequence of [negating] all knowledge.
This is a negation that is discriminating cognition;
it is not arrived at through perception;
neither in sequence nor in simultaneity
does such discriminating cognition [arise].
If [it arises] in the apprehension of non-discrimination —
true, but not of the discriminated [entities];
in non-apprehension, through the absence of attainment,
but prior to attainment, it is fitting.
[...lacuna...]
[...lacuna...]
And from the absence of both in dream,
discrimination of which [two entities] is ascertained?
If through being remembered, they are undiscriminated —
then sublation is obstructed;
all sublation would be of such a kind —
a subsequent cognition of a property in a property-bearer.
Therefore it is fitting: from sublating cognition
this verbal usage would arise;
even when the object is otherwise,
this form is cognized through the intellect.
In <s>ātma-khyāti</s> (self-cognition theory), they say everything is entirely internal;
in <s>śūnya-khyāti</s> (emptiness-cognition theory), some say it is simply empty;
in <s>akhyāti</s> (non-cognition theory), there is no distinction between reality and falsity;
therefore, [this is] the discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) of these errors (<s>vibhrama</s>).
